sentences: This is Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa.
It is smaller than many people expect, just 77 by 53 centimetres, painted on a panel of poplar wood.
Begin by taking in her whole figure and her calm, settled pose.
The sitter is generally identified as Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine merchant Francesco del Giocondo.
Vasari wrote that Leonardo took on the portrait for Francesco.
He began around 1503, but he never delivered the commission.
Leonardo kept the painting with him for more than a decade, adding layers.
Look closely and you will find no hard outlines on the face.
Using sfumato, he built up dozens of ultra-thin glazes so that light and shadow blend like smoke.
Let's move in to her eyes.
Their corners melt softly into shadow, so her expression is hard to pin down.
Notice too that her face has no visible eyebrows or lashes; one researcher argues they were lost to overcleaning.
Now drop your gaze to the corners of her mouth.
They are just as soft, so the smile seems to appear and disappear depending on whether you look at her mouth or her eyes.
That enigmatic smile has held viewers for centuries.
Turn to the landscape on the left side of the picture.
A winding road snakes between rocky hills, and above it lies a blue-grey lake.
Look carefully and you will see that the horizon here sits noticeably lower than on the right.
On the right, an arched bridge crosses the valley, and the horizon rises close to the level of her eyes.
Because the two sides do not quite match, the picture carries a quiet tension.
Apart from the road and bridge, there is little sign of people.
Look down at her folded hands.
Her right hand rests lightly on her left arm, creating a calm, reserved posture.
As on the face, the fingers are shaped by soft shadow rather than hard lines.
Step back and you will notice dark column bases at both edges.
She is seated in an open loggia, a kind of covered porch.
Early copies, and a sketch by Raphael, show these flanking columns far more clearly.
After Leonardo died in 1519, the painting passed to King Francis I of France.
It has hung in the Louvre since 1797.
On 21 August 1911 a Louvre employee, Vincenzo Peruggia, stole it, and its recovery two years later made it world-famous.
Today she greets crowds of visitors from behind bulletproof glass.
Before you go, let your eyes move between her mouth and her eyes.
Try to catch the moment when the smile is strongest, and the moment it slips away.
